messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 55
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 64

He is a 55-year-old African man who has spent most of his adult life doing work that requires a steady hand and a controlled face. As a bomb disposal technician, he is used to danger arriving in measured forms: a suspicious package, an unstable device, a crowd held back by tape and procedure. He knows how to move slowly, how to breathe, how to trust training when adrenaline starts to rise. What he does not know how to do, even now, is make sense of the morning the ground failed.

The disaster happens suddenly, during an ordinary stretch of life that still feels, in his telling, almost insulting in its normalcy. He is at work when news breaks of the storm—at first just another severe weather warning, then a growing urgency in the voices around him, then the realization that whole neighborhoods are flooding. By the time he reaches the affected area, the wind is already violent and the rain feels sharp against the skin. He remembers the sound of metal sheets snapping loose, trees cracking, people shouting names into the rain. His job that day is not to disable anything, but to help clear access, to move through wreckage, to assess what might remain dangerous after the waters recede.

He describes the chaos as worse than anything he has faced in his career because it is everywhere and nowhere at once. There is no single object to focus on, no clear perimeter to establish. Houses are split open. Cars sit half-submerged. Power lines lie in tangled lines across streets that have become rivers. He watches a child being carried from a roof and later sees an elderly man standing in chest-deep water, still trying to hold onto a plastic bag of documents that have long since dissolved. The images stay with him. In the weeks after, he finds that the details arrive uninvited: the color of the water, the smell of mud and fuel, the way people’s faces look when they realize everything they own is gone.

He tells himself at first that he is coping because he keeps working. He goes back to his shifts, checks equipment, speaks in the clipped language of safety protocols. He remains married, keeps his routines, sits at the table with his wife in the evenings. But his body has begun to live as if the storm is still coming. He is on alert before he is fully awake. He startles at sudden noise, especially sirens, thunder, or the heavy slam of a door. At night he sleeps lightly and wakes often, sometimes drenched in sweat, with the sense that water is rising around the bed. He checks the windows before dawn and walks the house more than once, as if he is still responsible for a perimeter that cannot be secured.

His wife notices first that he is no longer simply tired but distant. He becomes quieter, less patient, and more easily irritated by small interruptions. He avoids driving through flooded streets, then avoids the news, then avoids conversations about the disaster altogether. When people in his community speak about rebuilding, he nods but feels strangely detached, as though the future they are describing belongs to someone else. He struggles to enter damaged homes for work assignments after the disaster, and sometimes stands outside long enough for colleagues to ask if he is all right. He tells them he is fine. In private, he knows that “fine” has become a kind of disguise.

He also begins to feel shame about how little control he has over his own mind. In his profession, panic can get people killed. He has built a life around being the man who remains steady when others cannot. Now he finds himself gripping the edge of the sink while the image of floodwater in a hallway flashes through his mind. He forgets things, loses track of conversations, and gets angry at himself for not being able to simply push it away. At times he feels a hard knot in his chest that seems to warn him before memories even surface. He becomes more withdrawn, spending longer hours alone in the yard or sitting in the car before going inside.

What finally brings him to seek help is not a dramatic collapse, but a quiet moment that unsettles him more than he expects. After another night of poor sleep, he is standing in the kitchen when a sudden storm rolls through, and the sound of rain on the roof sends him into a full body jolt. He realizes he is no longer just remembering the disaster; he is living around it, arranging his days to avoid being caught off guard by weather, by noise, by anything that might flood him with the same helplessness. When his wife looks at him with concern and asks how long he has been carrying this alone, he admits that he is tired of pretending he can outrun it.
